narratives.narrative: Here nasa ('lift up', sense 101) appears in its rare negated form: the sense recorded is 'the soul not lifted to falsehood', and the type (102) is volition — this is not a bodily act but a movement of the will. The bearer (105) is the worshipper who may ascend the hill, and the operation (106) is a refusal: 'he does not lift up his soul to what is false or swear deceitfully — the self refuses to devote itself to an idol or a lie.' The target (107) is therefore given as undivided-devotion: what the refusal secures is a whole, single-hearted directedness. Coupling (112) ties the lift to 'soul-not-to-false', binding the will's motion to the object it declines. No source is recorded (103 present:false): the passage names no external cause pushing the soul — the movement issues from the interior's own governance. Seat is 'none' (104): this operation is not lodged in an organ; it is a state of the whole self, confirmed by locus (116) internal:ib-state. Manner is 'none' (108) — the refusal is stated without a described mode. Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113 present:false): the reader measures no degree of the will's resolve, adds no qualifier, traces no downstream consequence, and — notably — the refusal is framed as the worshipper's own characteristic (115) rather than an imposed command, so no prohibition dimension is recorded even though the content is a 'does not'. The discovery (114) crystallises it: the operation is 'a refusal of misdirected devotion: the interior will not give itself to emptiness or back a lie with an oath.' Read for the inner being, lifting the soul is here the very capacity to devote, exercised in the negative — the clean-handed, pure-hearted person is defined by where the soul is withheld.
narratives.story: This song asks who is fit to climb God's holy hill, and answers: the person whose inner life will not sell itself to a lie. The word for lifting up is turned around — instead of raising his soul toward something false, this worshipper refuses to. Nothing outside him forces the choice; it comes from his own settled will, and it is not felt in any one part of the body but is simply who he is inside. He will not pour his devotion into an empty idol, and he will not swear to back a falsehood. The picture is of a heart kept whole and single by everything it declines to give itself to.
narratives.variation_note: Alone among the ten nasa 'lift up' readings this one is negated (type = volition, not action): the soul is defined by refusing to be lifted to falsehood, so its target is undivided-devotion secured by withholding, rather than a positive raising of soul, hands, eyes or cup toward God.

narratives.narrative: The acrostic opens with nasa in its fullest interior sense (101): 'lift up my soul to you'. The type (102) is affect — an emotional, devotional lifting of the whole self, not a mere gesture. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the operation (106) is that 'the self lifts up its soul to God — the whole inner self raised toward him as the psalm opens.' The target (107) is self-offering: the lifting hands the person over. Coupling (112) is 'lift-up-soul', welding the act to its object, the soul itself. No source is recorded (103 present:false): the psalm names no prior cause; the movement is the psalmist's own initiating act of trust (note v2, 'in you I trust'). Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) is internal:ib-state — this is not organ-located but a condition of the entire interior. Manner is 'none' (108): no mode of the lifting is described. Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): the reader records no measured degree, no narrowing qualifier, and does not trace what the offering produces — the psalm states the self-surrender without quantifying or resolving it. Role (115) is characteristic: this defines the psalmist. The discovery (114) reads it as the acrostic 'handing the self over' from its first line. For the inner being, lifting up the soul is here the primary act of devotion — the whole self raised and given to God as the ground of the prayer that follows.
narratives.story: David begins his prayer by lifting his whole inner self up to God, like a man holding out everything he is with open hands. It is not just a gesture or a mood but the deep offering of himself, and it flows from his own trust rather than being triggered by anything outside him. This lifting is not felt in one part of him; it is the whole person turned upward and handed over. The prayer that follows rests on this opening act of self-surrender. From the very first line, he gives himself away to the God he trusts.
narratives.variation_note: Differs from the hand- and eye-liftings (63:4, 119:48, 121:1, 123:1, 134:2) in that the whole soul, not a body-part, is raised; and from the parallel soul-lifting at 86:4 in its type (affect here vs action there), reading the act as devotional feeling. Its target, self-offering, marks the positive counterpart to 24:4's negated withholding.

narratives.narrative: Here nasa carries its 'bear / endure' sense (101): 'then I could bear it'. The type (102) is action — a capacity exercised. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the operation (106) is to 'bear / endure (hypothetically)': the endurance is offered as a condition contrary to fact. The target (107) is a genuine pair (item_type pair, spans 280052->280051): 'an enemy's taunt' — what could be borne is a known foe's reproach. Coupling (112) is also a pair (280052->280057): the bearing is set beside 'hiding from an open adversary' — endurance and evasion are the two things open enmity would have permitted. No source is recorded (103 present:false): no external cause is named for the capacity to endure; it is the interior's own resilience. Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) internal:ib-state — the endurance is a state of the whole self, not organ-lodged. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): the reader records no measured degree of the endurance, no qualifier, and does not trace its outcome — because the outcome is precisely what the verse denies (it is not an enemy, so he cannot bear it). Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) is the sharp finding: nasa here is 'the capacity to shoulder a known foe's reproach — a strength that the betrayal of a friend dissolves, for there is no bracing against a trusted hand.' Read for the inner being, bearing is a real interior strength, but the passage exposes its limit: the self can carry open hostility and cannot carry treachery from a companion. The absence of any recorded effect underlines that the endurance never actually engages — betrayal has disarmed it.
narratives.story: The poet says something surprising about his own strength: if an enemy were mocking him, he could take it — he could brace himself and carry the insult, or simply keep out of the man's way. He has that kind of inner toughness for open hostility. But the pain here is not from an enemy at all; it is from a close friend who has turned on him. And against a trusted hand there is no bracing. The very strength that could have shouldered a foe's contempt collapses, because it was never built to carry betrayal.
narratives.variation_note: Among the four 'bear' readings this and 89:50 are endurance of reproach, while 126:6 (twice) is carrying a physical load. This one is uniquely hypothetical (a strength that does NOT engage, because the wound is a friend's, not a foe's), whereas 89:50 is an actual bearing of insult lodged in the heart.

narratives.narrative: This reading tracks the dark movement of the betrayer. The sense (101) is chalal, 'profane / violate': 'he violated his covenant'. Type (102) is action. The bearer (105) is the betrayer, and the operation (106) is to 'profane / break'. The target (107) is a pair (spans 280130->280132): 'his covenant' — the sworn bond itself is what is desecrated. Coupling (112) is another pair (280130->280126): the violation is welded to 'the hand stretched out against his friends' (v20a), so the inner faithlessness and the outward aggression are one motion. No source is recorded (103 present:false): the passage names no external cause driving the treachery — it issues from the betrayer's own interior, exposed in v21 as a heart at war behind smooth speech. Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) internal:ib-state: the profaning is not organ-located but a state of the whole self. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): the reader measures no degree, adds no qualifier, and traces no consequence here (the passage's judgement in v23 is God's separate act, not recorded as this operation's effect); and though the deed is covenant-breaking, no prohibition dimension is recorded — it is read as the betrayer's characteristic (115), what he is, not a rule he transgresses. The discovery (114) names it: 'the treachery of breaking a sworn covenant of friendship — faithlessness at its most defiling, the trust desecrated.' Read for the inner being with no valence bias, this is the interior of the traitor rendered fully: a self that can profane a sacred bond, its smooth words drawn swords, treated with the same descriptive weight as the psalms of trust.
narratives.story: The betrayer in this psalm does something worse than attack — he desecrates. He had sworn friendship, and now he tramples that sacred promise underfoot, stretching out his hand against the very people he had bound himself to. The wound and the words come from one poisoned source inside him: his speech is smooth as butter while war fills his heart. Nothing outside him made him do it; the treachery is simply who he has become. This is the poem's unflinching look at a friend's inner life gone rotten — trust turned into a drawn sword.
narratives.variation_note: Of the two 'violate' (chalal) readings, this is the profaning of a personal covenant of friendship by a human betrayer (target = his covenant, coupled to the hand against friends), whereas 89:31 is David's children violating God's statutes — a shift of bearer (friend vs sons) and target (a friendship-bond vs God's ordinances).

narratives.narrative: Here nasa is the bodily posture of prayer: sense (101) 'lift up (the hands)', type (102) action. Uniquely in this family the seat (104) is filled — 'the hands' — so this lifting IS organ-located, and correspondingly the locus (116) is external:god: the movement reaches outward toward God rather than resting as an internal state. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, the operation (106) is to 'lift up (the hands in worship)', and the target (107) is 'to God, in his name'. Manner (108) is filled too — 'in God's name' — the mode under which the hands rise. Coupling (112) is a pair (281058->281054): the raised hands are welded to 'the gesture of the lifelong blessing' (v4a, 'so I will bless you as long as I live'). No source is recorded (103 present:false): the psalm names no external trigger; the lifting flows from the thirsting, love-driven soul of vv1-3. Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, or downstream result is recorded — the worship is stated, not measured. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads the raised hands as 'the outward act of a heart lifted to God, worship enacted with the whole self.' For the inner being, this is the interior movement of blessing taking bodily form: the seat in the hands and the external locus show devotion breaking out of the self and into gesture, God being the arena the whole person reaches toward.
narratives.story: In a dry, waterless wilderness, thirsting for God, David turns his longing into a gesture: he lifts his hands in worship, in God's own name. Here the lifting is something you can see — it lives in the hands and stretches outward toward God, not just inside the heart. It rises out of a soul already full of love and praise, and it belongs to a lifelong habit of blessing him. The inward devotion has become a bodily act. His whole self, hands and heart together, reaches up toward the God he cannot stop praising.
narratives.variation_note: This is the only 'lift up' reading with a filled seat ('the hands') and a filled manner ('in God's name'), and its locus is external:god rather than internal:ib-state. It differs from the soul-liftings (25:1, 86:4, 143:8) by being an outward bodily gesture, and shares the hand-lifting motif with 119:48 and 134:2.

narratives.narrative: This reading uses a different verb, rum ('lift up / exalt', sense 101), and turns the family's motif toward pride. Type (102) is action. The bearer (105) is the wicked, and the operation (106) is to 'lift up the horn (forbidden self-exaltation)'. The target (107) is a pair (282722->282723): 'the horn (symbol of strength/pride)' — the self-promoting emblem raised. Manner (108) is filled: 'on high, with haughty neck', the arrogant mode of the gesture. Coupling (112) is a pair (282722->282729): the raised horn is welded to 'speaking with haughty neck' (v5) — proud posture and proud speech are one movement. No source is recorded (103 present:false): the passage names no cause outside the wicked; the exaltation wells up from their own interior. Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) internal:ib-state — the pride is a state of the whole self, not organ-lodged. Intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): notably, though the verse is a command ('Do not lift up your horn'), the reader records no prohibition dimension — the self-exaltation is read as the wicked's characteristic (115), the interior disposition being addressed, and no measured degree, qualifier, or effect is traced (the counter-movement, God's putting down and lifting up in v7, is a separate divine act). The discovery (114) names it: 'the arrogant self-exaltation God forbids... self-promotion the wicked must abandon, for lifting up is God's to give (v7).' Read with no valence bias, this is the inner being of pride laid bare and given full weight: a self that raises its own strength on high — the dark mirror of the psalter's upward devotion, and forbidden precisely because exaltation belongs to God.
narratives.story: To the arrogant and the wicked the psalm says plainly: stop raising your horn. Lifting the horn was the proud swagger of self-made strength, chin up, neck stiff, boasting with the mouth what the posture already declared. This pride comes from nowhere but inside them — it is simply what they are. And the psalm sets a hard limit on it: no one lifts himself up; it is God who lowers one man and raises another. Here the study looks squarely at the interior of pride, the very opposite of the humble soul lifted to God, and finds it forbidden because exaltation was never ours to hand ourselves.
narratives.variation_note: The two rum 'lift up' readings diverge sharply: here the wicked's forbidden self-exaltation (bearer = the wicked, manner = haughty, a descent/pride movement), against 110:7 where the same verb marks the king's God-given triumph (bearer = the king, an ascent). The difference — condemned pride vs granted victory — is the finding: lifting up is illegitimate when self-taken, legitimate when God-given.

narratives.narrative: Here nasa lifts the soul again: sense (101) 'lift up (nasa)', with the operation (106) 'lift up the soul'. Type (102) is action. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, the target (107) is 'to God', and the locus (116) is external:god — the soul's raising is read as directed outward toward God. Coupling (112) welds the lift to 'the soul gladdened' (v4a, 'Gladden the soul of your servant'): the lifting of the soul upward and the plea for its gladdening are bound together, so the upward reach is also a reach for joy. No source is recorded (103 present:false): no external cause is named; the movement is the servant's own devotion, grounded in his need (v1, 'poor and needy'). Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): the reader records no degree, qualifier, or outcome — the raising is stated as an act of the whole self, not measured. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) names it 'the aspiration of the whole self toward God, devotion as upward reach.' For the inner being, lifting the soul here is dependence turned upward: the needy servant raises his whole interior to God as the ground of his plea, and the lifting is inseparable from his longing for the gladness only God can give.
narratives.story: A man who calls himself poor and needy prays for gladness, and the reason he gives is that he lifts up his whole soul to God. His inner self reaches upward, out toward God, and that reaching is the same motion as his longing for joy — he raises his heart to the only one who can lighten it. Nothing pushes him to do this from outside; it rises out of his own need and devotion. This is what dependence looks like from the inside: the whole self stretched up to God, asking to be made glad.
narratives.variation_note: Like 25:1 and 143:8 this raises the whole soul to God, but its recorded type is action (not affect) and its locus is external:god (not internal:ib-state), and its distinctive coupling binds the lifting to the plea to have the soul 'gladdened' — devotion driven by need for joy rather than pure self-offering.

narratives.narrative: This reading breaks the lift/bear pattern with teruah, the 'festal shout' (sense 101), type (102) action. The bearer (105) is 'the people', the operation (106) is to 'raise the festal shout', and the target (107) is 'to God the king'. No source is recorded (103 present:false): the passage names no external trigger — the acclamation rises from the people's own knowledge of God (v15, 'Blessed are the people who know the festal shout'). Seat is 'none' (104): the shout is not organ-located but is the whole people's act. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, or downstream result is recorded — the acclamation is stated, not measured. Two dimensions carry values that read as cross-references rather than descriptions: coupling (112) is recorded as 'external:god' and locus (116) as 'paired with knowing and walking in the light' — that is, the shout is welded to its Godward direction and set beside the interior knowing and the walking 'in the light of your face' (v15). This means the jubilant cry is not a bare noise but the outward face of an inner state: the people who KNOW the shout are those whose walk is lit by God's presence. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) reads it as 'the joyful acclamation of God as king, worship as jubilant cry.' For the inner being, the shout is joy breaking into voice — an interior gladness and knowledge of God-as-king that cannot stay silent, the corporate counterpart to the individual soul lifted in the other readings.
narratives.story: The happy people in this psalm are the ones who know the festal shout — the great glad cry that hails God as their king. It bursts out of them not because anyone commands it but because they know him; the joy inside simply has to be voiced. And this shout is not empty noise: it belongs together with a life walked in the light of God's face. To know the shout is to walk in his presence and be glad. Here a whole community's inner joy overflows into a single jubilant cry to their King.

narratives.narrative: The second chalal reading (sense 101 'violate', type 102 action) is set within God's own conditional warning about David's line. The bearer (105) is 'David's children', the operation (106) is to 'profane / violate', and the target (107) is 'God's statutes' (v31, 'if they violate my statutes'). Coupling (112) welds the violation to 'not keeping his commandments' (v31b): the profaning and the neglect are one disobedient motion. Locus (116) is external:god — the offence is against God's ordinances, so its arena is Godward, not a merely internal state. No source is recorded (103 present:false): no external cause is named for the children's disobedience; it would issue from their own interior. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): the reader records no degree, qualifier, or effect — and though violating statutes is transgression, no prohibition dimension is logged, because the operation is read as the disposition itself (role 115, characteristic), the potential faithlessness of the sons, not the rule they would break (God's consequence, the rod of v32, is a separate divine act). The discovery (114) names it 'the profaning of God's ordinances by the sons.' For the inner being, this is faithlessness projected as a possibility: a self that could desecrate what God has commanded, held up here — with no valence softening — alongside God's countervailing vow never to violate his own covenant (v34), so the human capacity to profane is measured against the divine refusal to do the same.
narratives.story: God makes a promise about David's descendants, and inside it lies a warning: if his children trample on God's laws and refuse to keep his commands, they will be disciplined. Breaking the rules and ignoring them are really the same faithless move, and it is aimed at what God has ordained. Such disobedience would come from within the sons themselves. What makes it strike harder is the contrast the psalm draws: the sons might desecrate their part of the bond, yet God swears he will never desecrate his. The human power to break faith is shown up against God's steady refusal to do so.
narratives.variation_note: Set against 55:20's violation of a personal friendship-covenant, this reading has David's children as bearer and God's statutes as target, and its locus is external:god (not internal:ib-state): the profaning is disobedience toward God's ordinances rather than treachery toward a human friend, and it sits inside God's own conditional warning rather than a lament over betrayal.

narratives.narrative: Here nasa is inward carrying: sense (101) 'bear (nasa)', type (102) action. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, the operation (106) is to 'bear / carry', and the target (107) is 'the insults of the nations in the heart' (v50, 'how I bear in my heart the insults of all the many nations'). No source is recorded (103 present:false): no external cause is named for the bearing — the reproach is simply lodged and carried within. Seat is 'none' (104): though the verse says 'in my heart', the reader records no organ-seat for the operation itself, treating it as a state of the whole self rather than a faculty. Two dimensions carry cross-reference values: coupling (112) is recorded as 'internal:ib-state' and locus (116) as 'paired with the servants' being mocked' — the private carrying is bound to an inner condition and set beside the public humiliation of God's servants (v50a), so the individual's borne shame stands for the whole community's. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): the reader records no degree of the burden, no qualifier, and no relief or outcome — the weight is stated as still-carried, unresolved, which fits the psalm's unanswered lament. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) names it 'the inward carrying of reproach, humiliation lodged in the heart.' For the inner being, bearing here is the opposite pole from the endurance of 55:12: there the strength did not engage; here the reproach is actually taken up and held inside, an ongoing interior weight of shame borne on behalf of God's mocked servants.
narratives.story: The poet cries out that he carries something heavy inside him: the insults of many nations, lodged right in his heart. No one is forcing it on him in the moment — the shame is simply there, and he bears it. And he does not carry it only for himself; his private humiliation stands in for the mockery heaped on all of God's servants. The psalm never lifts the weight or answers the taunts; it ends with the burden still held. This is what it looks like to carry reproach on the inside, an ache of shame taken up and not put down.
narratives.variation_note: Both this and 55:12 are 'bearing' as endurance of reproach, but here the insult is actually carried inside the heart (an ongoing, real burden borne for the mocked servants), whereas 55:12 is a hypothetical strength that never engages because the wound came from a friend. Against 126:6's carrying of seed and sheaves, this is an inward emotional load, not a physical one.

narratives.narrative: This rum reading is triumph, not pride: sense (101) 'lift up (rum)', and — distinctively in this family — type (102) is state, not action. The operation is not something worked but a condition arrived at. The bearer (105) is 'the king', the operation (106) is to 'lift up his head', and the target (107) is 'in triumph'. No source is recorded (103 present:false): the passage names no external agent of the lifting in the operation itself, though the surrounding psalm makes clear it follows God's shattering of the king's foes (vv5-6) — the raised head is the aftermath of victory, not a self-taken exaltation. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, or further effect is recorded — the lifted head IS the culminating state. Two dimensions carry cross-reference values: coupling (112) is 'external:god' and locus (116) 'paired with drinking from the brook by the way' (v7a) — the triumph is bound to its Godward frame and set beside the image of the king pausing to drink mid-pursuit before raising his head. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) names it 'the king's triumphant exaltation, head raised in victory after God has shattered his foes.' For the inner being, lifting the head here is the interior posture of vindicated victory — the settled state of one lifted up by God, the legitimate counterpart to the forbidden self-exaltation of 75:4.
narratives.story: At the end of the battle psalm, the king pauses to drink from a stream along the road, and then he lifts his head high in triumph. This raising is not something he strains to do; it is simply the state he ends up in — the settled posture of a victor. And it comes only after God has shattered his enemies for him, so his lifted head is the fruit of God's help, not proud swagger. The picture is quiet and total: refreshed, victorious, his head raised. This is the honest, granted kind of being lifted up — the very thing pride tries to seize for itself but never truly earns.
narratives.variation_note: The two rum readings are opposites: here the king's God-given triumph (bearer = the king, type = state, an ascent following God's victory), against 75:4's forbidden self-exaltation of the wicked (bearer = the wicked, type = action, manner = haughty). Legitimate lifting-up is received from God; illegitimate lifting-up is seized by the proud self.

narratives.narrative: Here nasa lifts an object of thanksgiving: sense (101) 'lift up (nasa)', type (102) action, operation (106) 'lift up'. The bearer (105) is the psalmist and the target (107) is 'the cup of salvation' (v13). No source is recorded (103 present:false): no external cause is named; the gesture rises from the psalmist's own gratitude for rescue. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): the reader records no degree, qualifier, or downstream outcome — the thankful act is stated, not measured. Two dimensions carry cross-reference values: coupling (112) is 'external:god' and locus (116) 'paired with calling on God's name' (v13b, 'and call on the name of the Lord') — the raised cup is welded to its Godward direction and set beside the act of invoking God's name, so the lifting and the calling are one movement of grateful worship. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) names it 'the thankful gesture, raising the cup in acknowledgement of God's rescue.' For the inner being, this lifting externalises gratitude: the interior response to salvation takes the form of a raised cup and a called name, devotion made public in the presence of all God's people (v14). Unlike the soul-liftings, the self here does not raise itself but raises a token of what God has done — thanks turned into gesture.
narratives.story: Saved from death, the poet reaches for a cup — the cup of salvation — and lifts it high while he calls out God's name. The raising of the cup and the calling of the name are one act of thanks, flowing straight from his gratitude for being rescued. Nothing outside prompts it; the relief inside him simply spills over into this gesture. Here he does not lift himself; he lifts a token of what God has done for him, and he does it openly, before all God's people. It is thankfulness made visible — a toast of rescue offered back to the Rescuer.
narratives.variation_note: Unlike the readings that raise the self (soul: 25:1, 86:4, 143:8) or the body (hands: 63:4, 119:48, 134:2; eyes: 121:1, 123:1), here the object lifted is the cup of salvation — a token of God's rescue, so the lifting expresses thanksgiving for what God has done rather than the self reaching upward in devotion or dependence.

narratives.narrative: Here nasa raises the hands toward God's word: sense (101) 'lift up (nasa)', type (102) action, operation (106) 'lift up the hands'. The bearer (105) is the psalmist and the target (107) is 'God's word' — specifically the commandments he loves (v48, 'I will lift up my hands toward your commandments, which I love'). No source is recorded (103 present:false): no external cause is named; the gesture flows from the love and delight of the surrounding verses (v47, 'I find my delight in your commandments, which I love'). Seat is 'none' (104): although hands are named, the reader records no organ-seat for the operation itself, reading it as an act of the whole devoted self. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, or outcome is recorded. Coupling (112) is 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm' — a cross-reference noting that this lifting belongs to the long, sustained devotion running through Psalm 119 rather than to a single isolated moment. Locus (116) is external:god. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) names it 'the lifted hands of devotion toward the loved commandments.' For the inner being, this is striking: the gesture normally aimed at God is here aimed at his commandments — love for God's word draws the same bodily posture of worship, so the interior affection for the law becomes indistinguishable from devotion to God himself. Meditation follows in the same verse ('I will meditate on your statutes'), binding the outward lift to inward pondering.
narratives.story: The poet loves God's commands so deeply that he lifts his hands toward them, the way a worshipper reaches out to God himself. The gesture pours out of pure delight — he loves these commands, and his body follows his heart. This is not a one-off; it belongs to a whole life of devotion that runs all through this long psalm. And the raised hands lead straight into quiet reflection, as he turns the same statutes over in his mind. Love for God's word here looks exactly like love for God: hands lifted, heart pondering, the whole self drawn toward what he treasures.
narratives.variation_note: Shares the hand-lifting gesture with 63:4 and 134:2, but its target is God's word (the loved commandments) rather than God directly or the holy place, and its coupling uniquely marks it as part of the sustained devotional arc of Psalm 119 rather than a single moment — love for the law drawing the posture usually reserved for God himself.

narratives.narrative: Here nasa raises the eyes: sense (101) 'lift up the eyes (nasa)', type (102) action, operation (106) 'lift up the eyes'. The bearer (105) is the psalmist and the target (107) is 'to seek help' (v1, 'I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come?'). No source is recorded (103 present:false): no external cause is named; the lifting arises from the pilgrim's own need, the question of where help will come from. Seat is 'none' (104): though eyes are named, the reader logs no organ-seat for the operation, treating it as an act of the whole seeking self. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, or outcome is recorded at the act itself — the answer (v2, 'My help comes from the Lord') comes as the psalm's reply, not as a recorded effect of the operation. Coupling (112) is 'external:god' and locus (116) 'paired with the help that comes from the Lord' — the raised eyes are bound to their Godward direction and set beside the psalm's answer, so the seeking look and the found help form one movement. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) names it 'the seeking gaze of the pilgrim, looking beyond the hills to God for help.' For the inner being, lifting the eyes is dependence enacted as a look: the interior need turns outward and upward, scanning past the hills to fix on God as the only source of help — attention itself becoming an act of trust.
narratives.story: A traveller lifts his eyes to the hills and asks the honest question of the anxious: where is my help going to come from? The lifted gaze is his need made visible — his whole attention turns outward, searching. And the psalm answers him at once: his help comes from the Lord, the Maker of heaven and earth. So the seeking look and the found help belong together, one movement from question to assurance. To raise the eyes like this is simply to depend on God with your whole attention, looking past every hill to the One who keeps you.
narratives.variation_note: Shares the eye-lifting motif with 123:1, but here the eyes rise 'to the hills' as a searching question ('from where does my help come?'), targeting the seeking of help, whereas 123:1 fixes directly on God enthroned and targets mercy. This is the gaze that seeks; 123:1 is the gaze that waits.

narratives.narrative: Here nasa again raises the eyes, but toward the enthroned God: sense (101) 'lift up the eyes (nasa)', type (102) action, operation (106) 'lift up the eyes'. The bearer (105) is the psalmist and the target (107) is 'to God enthroned' (v1, 'To you I lift up my eyes, O you who are enthroned in the heavens'). No source is recorded (103 present:false): no external cause is named; the lifting flows from the dependent posture the psalm develops. Seat is 'none' (104): eyes are named but no organ-seat is logged for the operation; it is the whole waiting self. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, or outcome is recorded at the act. Coupling (112) is 'external:god' and locus (116) 'paired with the servant's upward look for mercy' — the raised eyes are bound Godward and set beside the psalm's own image (v2) of servants watching the hand of their master 'till he has mercy upon us'. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) names it 'the upward look of dependence, eyes raised to the enthroned God for mercy.' For the inner being, this lifting is patient dependence: the interior, wearied by contempt (vv3-4), fixes its gaze on God as a servant watches a master's hand — not scanning for help but steadily waiting on mercy. The look is sustained attention, trust that will not drop its eyes until God acts.
narratives.story: Worn down by scorn and contempt, the poet lifts his eyes straight up to God on his throne. He compares it to the way servants keep their eyes on their master's hand, and a maid on her mistress's, watching and waiting for the smallest sign of favour. His look is not a quick, searching glance but a steady, patient gaze that refuses to look away until mercy comes. Nothing forces this posture; it grows out of his weariness and his trust. To lift the eyes here is to wait on God with quiet, fixed dependence, holding the gaze until he shows kindness.
narratives.variation_note: Shares the eye-lifting motif with 121:1, but fixes directly on God 'enthroned in the heavens' and targets mercy through patient waiting (the servant watching the master's hand), whereas 121:1 raises the eyes 'to the hills' as a searching question about where help comes from. This is the gaze that waits; 121:1 is the gaze that seeks.

narratives.narrative: Here nasa is physical carrying charged with grief: sense (101) 'bear (nasa)', type (102) action, operation (106) 'carry the seed out'. The bearer (105) is 'the sower' and the target (107) is 'in grief' (v6, 'He who goes out weeping, bearing the seed for sowing'). No source is recorded (103 present:false): no external cause is named for the burden; the sower simply goes out carrying it. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located — this is a bodily load, but the reader logs it as the whole person's act rather than a faculty. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, or immediate outcome is recorded at the act itself — the reversal (v6b, coming home with joy) is narrated separately as the paired return, not as this operation's traced effect. Coupling (112) is 'internal:ib-state' and locus (116) 'paired with bringing sheaves home' — the carrying is bound to an inner condition (the weeping) and set beside the joyful return-load of the sowing's other half. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) names it 'the burdened going-out, carrying the precious seed to be given up to the ground.' For the inner being, bearing here is grief in motion: the interior sorrow ('weeping', 'tears', v5) is embodied in a literal burden carried out to be surrendered — the seed given up to the earth. It is loss enacted, the heavy first half of a movement whose second half (the return) is joy.
narratives.story: A farmer walks out to his field in tears, carrying the seed he is about to bury in the ground. The load in his arms matches the sorrow in his chest — going out weeping, hauling the precious seed only to give it up to the soil. This is grief you can see: the heavy, reluctant walk of someone letting go of what he values with no guarantee yet in hand. It is the sad first half of the story. Everything about it is loss carried outward, the burden of sowing before any harvest is in sight.
narratives.variation_note: This and its twin at the same verse (bear#4) form a deliberate pair: here the going-out is burdened with grief ('in tears', target = in grief), carrying seed to give up to the ground, whereas #4 is the joyful return carrying sheaves. The same arms and the same verb hold sorrow on the way out and joy on the way back — the contrast is the point. Both differ from 55:12 and 89:50, where 'bearing' is endurance of reproach rather than a physical load.

narratives.narrative: The companion reading at the same verse carries the harvest: sense (101) 'bring (nasa)', type (102) action, operation (106) 'carry the sheaves home'. The bearer (105) is again 'the sower' and the target (107) is 'in joy' (v6b, 'shall come home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves with him'). No source is recorded (103 present:false): no external cause is named at the act; the return-load is simply borne. Seat is 'none' (104): not organ-located, a bodily burden read as the whole person's act. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, or further outcome is recorded — this carrying IS the culminating joy. Coupling (112) is 'internal:ib-state' and locus (116) 'paired with bearing the seed out' — the joyful load is bound to an inner condition (the shouts of joy) and explicitly set against the grieving going-out of its twin. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) names it precisely: 'the joyful return-burden, the same arms that carried seed in tears now full of sheaves.' For the inner being, bearing here is joy embodied — the identical action of carrying, but now the interior condition has flipped from weeping to shouting, and the load has changed from surrendered seed to gathered harvest. The two readings preserve one truth the passage will not let collapse: the very act that was grief on the way out becomes gladness on the way home.
narratives.story: The same farmer who trudged out weeping now comes home shouting for joy, his arms full of grain. It is the very same act of carrying — but everything inside him has changed, from tears to celebration, and the load has changed from buried seed to gathered harvest. What he gave up to the ground in sorrow now returns to him as reward. The heavy walk out and the glad walk back are two halves of one story, and the poem keeps them side by side on purpose. The burden that once meant loss now means fullness and joy.
narratives.variation_note: The twin of bear#3 at the same verse: here the return is joyful (target = in joy), carrying sheaves home, against #3's grieving going-out carrying seed. Same bearer, same verb, opposite inner condition — the deliberate grief-to-joy reversal is the finding. Both differ from the endurance-of-reproach 'bearings' at 55:12 and 89:50 by being a physical load.

narratives.narrative: This reading uses gabah in negated form (sense 101, 'lifted up (gabah, negated)'), and its type (102) is disposition — uniquely in this family it names a settled inner bearing rather than an action or state. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the operation (106) is 'not exalt the heart' (v1, 'my heart is not lifted up'). The target (107) is 'in pride' — the pride the heart is kept from. No source is recorded (103 present:false): no external cause is named; the restraint issues from the psalmist's own cultivated disposition (v2, 'I have calmed and quieted my soul'). Seat is 'none' (104): though the heart is named, no organ-seat is logged for the operation — it is read as a state of the whole self, confirmed by locus (116) internal:ib-state. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, or outcome is recorded — and though the content is self-denial, no prohibition dimension is logged, because this humility is read as the psalmist's characteristic (115), what he is, not a rule imposed. Coupling (112) is 'internal:ib-state', and the locus value adds it is 'paired with the unproud heart'. The discovery (114) names it 'the pride deliberately negated, the heart kept from rising.' For the inner being, this is humility as active restraint: the same upward motion that the family celebrates when directed to God is here refused when it would be self-exaltation. The heart that could swell is deliberately kept low — an interior discipline, the mirror-image of 75:4's forbidden self-lifting, chosen from within rather than commanded from without.
narratives.story: David quietly tells God what his inner life is like: my heart is not puffed up. There is a lift the proud heart makes, swelling with its own importance, and he simply does not make it — he keeps his heart low on purpose. This is not a rule forced on him but a settled way of being he has cultivated, the fruit of a calmed and quieted soul. The same rising motion that is beautiful when the soul reaches up to God becomes pride when it reaches up for itself, and that he refuses. His humility is a chosen stillness, a heart that could swell but chooses not to.

narratives.narrative: Paired with the negated heart in the same verse, this reading negates rum applied to the eyes: sense (101) 'raise the eyes (rum, negated)', type (102) action, operation (106) 'not raise the eyes too high' (v1, 'my eyes are not raised too high'). The bearer (105) is the psalmist and the target (107) is 'in ambition' — the over-reaching the gaze is kept from. No source is recorded (103 present:false): no external cause is named; the restraint is self-imposed. Seat is 'none' (104): eyes are named but no organ-seat is logged for the operation; it is a state of the whole self, confirmed by locus (116) internal:ib-state. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, or outcome is recorded, and no prohibition dimension despite the self-restraint — it is read as the psalmist's characteristic (115). Coupling (112) is 'internal:ib-state', and the locus value notes it is 'paired with not occupying with great things' (v1c, 'I do not occupy myself with things too great and too marvelous for me'). The discovery (114) names it 'the operation of restraint: the gaze kept from reaching above its station.' For the inner being, this preserves a distinction the passage will not collapse: the humble heart (the gabah reading) and the humble eyes (this rum reading) are two facets of one disposition, but they are kept separate — the heart refuses to swell, the gaze refuses to climb. Read against the family's Godward eye-liftings (121:1, 123:1), the irony is sharp: the very act of raising the eyes is good when it seeks God and reined in when it reaches, ambitiously, above one's station.
narratives.story: In the same breath, David adds that his eyes are not raised too high — he does not let his gaze climb above where he belongs, reaching for things too big and too dazzling for him. Alongside a heart that will not swell, here is a look that will not overreach; together they make one humble spirit, though the poem keeps them as two distinct restraints. He chooses this himself; nothing outside curbs him. And there is a quiet irony in it: lifting the eyes is a beautiful thing when it looks up to God for help, but the same lifting becomes proud ambition when it strains after greatness beyond one's place. So he keeps his eyes low and his soul at rest.

narratives.narrative: Here nasa is a summons to corporate worship: sense (101) 'lift up the hands (nasa)', type (102) action, operation (106) 'lift up the hands'. The bearer (105) is 'the servants' — those who stand by night in the house of the Lord (v1) — so this lifting is plural and communal. The target (107) is 'to the holy place' (v2, 'Lift up your hands to the holy place and bless the Lord'). No source is recorded (103 present:false): no external cause is named; the gesture answers the call to bless. Seat is 'none' (104): hands are named but no organ-seat is logged for the operation, which is read as the servants' whole-self act of worship. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, or outcome is recorded — the gesture is commanded and stated, not measured. Coupling (112) is 'external:god' and locus (116) 'paired with blessing the Lord' — the raised hands are bound Godward and welded to the act of blessing (v2b), so the physical lifting and the verbal blessing are one worship. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) names it 'the gesture of worship: hands raised toward the sanctuary, the body enacting the blessing.' For the inner being, this lifting is worship made corporate and bodily: the servants' interior devotion, gathered in the night watches, breaks into a shared physical posture directed at the holy place — the community's blessing of God enacted with the whole body, hands lifted as the visible form of an inward reverence.
narratives.story: This short psalm calls out to the night-time servants in God's house: come, lift your hands toward the sanctuary and bless the Lord. It is a summons to a whole group, and their answer is a shared gesture — many hands raised together toward the holy place. The lifting of the hands and the blessing on their lips are one and the same act of worship, the body doing what the heart means. Their quiet night-watch devotion becomes visible and communal, arms stretched up in the dark toward God. It is reverence you can see, a congregation blessing God with lifted hands.
narratives.variation_note: Shares the hand-lifting gesture with 63:4 and 119:48, but its bearer is plural ('the servants', a corporate summons in the night watches) and its target is 'the holy place', with the lifting welded to blessing the Lord — communal, sanctuary-directed worship rather than an individual's raised hands toward God (63:4) or toward the loved commandments (119:48).

narratives.narrative: The family's last reading returns to lifting the soul: sense (101) 'lift up the soul', and — like 25:1 — type (102) is affect, a devotional lifting of the whole inner self. The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the operation (106) is that 'the whole soul is lifted toward God — the self offered upward as the ground of the plea.' The target (107) is self-offering. Coupling (112) is 'lift-the-soul', welding the act to its object. No source is recorded (103 present:false): no external cause is named; the lifting rises from the psalmist's own trust (v8a, 'in you I trust'). Seat is 'none' (104) and locus (116) internal:ib-state — not organ-located but a condition of the entire interior. Manner is 'none' (108); intensity, specifier, effect and prohibition are all absent (109/110/111/113): no degree, qualifier, or downstream result is recorded — the self-surrender is stated as the ground of the prayer, not measured. Role (115) is characteristic. The discovery (114) names it 'the raising of the entire inner self as an oblation of trust.' For the inner being, this lifting is trust in extremity: unlike the untroubled opening of 25:1, here the soul is lifted from a crushed and fainting condition (v3-4, 'my spirit faints within me; my heart within me is appalled'; v7, 'my spirit fails'). The same upward self-offering is made not out of settled devotion but out of desperation — the whole failing interior raised to God as the very basis on which the psalmist asks to be shown the way (v8b) and rescued. Lifting the soul is here the last act of a spirit at the end of itself, still directing its whole self toward God.
narratives.story: By the end of this desperate prayer, the poet's spirit is fainting and his heart is appalled — he feels crushed, close to the grave. And yet, out of that collapse, he lifts his whole soul up to God. He raises his failing inner self as his one offering, the very reason he dares to ask God to show him the way and save his life. It is the same handing-over of the soul that a calmer psalm makes in peace, but here it is made from the edge of despair. Even emptied and exhausted, he turns everything he has left upward, trusting God with the whole of himself.
narratives.variation_note: Like 25:1 this lifts the whole soul to God as self-offering with type affect and locus internal:ib-state, but the context differs decisively: 25:1 opens in settled trust, whereas here the soul is lifted from a fainting, crushed, near-death condition (vv3-7) — the same upward self-surrender made out of desperation rather than composure. It differs from the action-type soul-lifting at 86:4 by being devotional feeling, not a stated act.
